pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Outline approaches to waste management in promoting sustainable management.
- Conduct a survey of a community's waste management practices and present a report.

pages.title: What is Waste Management?
pages.body: Waste management is the collection, handling, treatment and disposal of unwanted materials produced by households, businesses, farms and industries. Sustainable waste management goes further than simply removing waste from sight. It aims to handle waste in ways that protect human health and the environment, while also conserving resources for future use, rather than allowing waste to pile up, pollute water sources, or release harmful substances into the air and soil.

pages.title: Approaches to Sustainable Waste Management
pages.body:
Reducing, reusing, recycling, composting and safe disposal are five key approaches that together promote sustainable waste management, as summarised in the table below.

| **APPROACH** | **DESCRIPTION** | **EXAMPLE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Reducing** | Cutting down the amount of waste produced in the first place | Buying only what is needed and avoiding excess packaging |
| **Reusing** | Using an item again for the same or a different purpose instead of throwing it away | Reusing glass bottles or containers for storage |
| **Recycling** | Processing waste materials so they can be made into new products | Turning waste paper into new paper products, or plastic into new plastic items |
| **Composting** | Allowing organic waste, such as food and plant matter, to decompose into useful manure | Turning kitchen and garden waste into compost for growing crops |
| **Safe disposal** | Properly collecting, transporting and disposing of waste that cannot be reduced, reused or recycled | Using designated landfill sites rather than open dumping or burning |

pages.title: Why Sustainable Waste Management Matters
pages.body: Protecting public health, preventing environmental pollution, and conserving natural resources are three major reasons sustainable waste management is important for any community. Poorly managed waste can block drains and cause flooding, provide breeding grounds for disease carrying pests such as flies and mosquitoes, contaminate drinking water sources, and release harmful gases when burned in the open. By contrast, well managed waste, particularly through reducing, reusing, recycling and composting, reduces these risks while also saving materials and energy that would otherwise be needed to produce new resources from scratch.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Types of Waste and Sorting at Source

pages.title: Types of Waste and Sorting at Source
pages.body:
| **TYPE OF WASTE** | **MEANING** | **EXAMPLES** | **BEST WAY TO HANDLE IT** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Biodegradable waste** | Waste that is broken down by microorganisms and rots | Food scraps, leaves, paper, animal droppings | Make it into compost or use it to produce biogas |
| **Non biodegradable waste** | Waste that does not rot for a very long time | Plastics, glass, metal cans | Reduce its use, reuse it or send it for recycling |
| **Hazardous waste** | Waste that can harm health or the environment | Batteries, old medicines, used syringes, pesticide containers, old phones and computers | Keep it separate and hand it to a special collection service. Never burn or bury it at home |

Sorting at source means putting each type of waste into a separate, labelled bin at the place where it is produced. Sorted waste is clean and easy to compost or recycle, while mixed waste usually ends up at a dump site. Burning waste in the open releases smoke and poisonous gases that harm the lungs. An incinerator is a special furnace that burns waste at a very high temperature. It greatly reduces the volume of waste, but it must be well controlled so that it does not pollute the air.

pages.title: Look at the picture
pages.body:
[[img:i6e163ca28|Fig 5.1  The waste management hierarchy, showing the most preferred approaches at the top and the least preferred at the bottom]]

Notice that reducing waste in the first place is considered the most preferred approach, since it prevents waste from being created at all, while disposal is considered the least preferred approach, since it deals with waste only after all other options have been exhausted. A sustainable waste management system tries to apply the higher, more preferred approaches as much as possible before relying on final disposal.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Many Ghanaian cities and towns face particular challenges with plastic waste, since plastic takes a very long time to break down naturally and can block drains, harm animals, and pollute water bodies. Community led initiatives that collect and recycle plastic waste, alongside national policies aimed at reducing single use plastics, are examples of how sustainable waste management approaches are being applied at different levels, from individual households to entire cities.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Applying Waste Management Practices in a Community

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Carry out an activity to manage waste using knowledge acquired on sustainable waste management practices in your community.
- Evaluate the waste management practices carried out in a community and present a report.

pages.title: From Knowledge to Action
pages.body: Having learnt about sustainable waste management approaches in Lesson 1, this lesson focuses on actually applying that knowledge through a practical, hands on activity within your own community. Turning knowledge into action is an important scientific and civic skill, since understanding a concept in theory is only truly useful once it is applied to solve a real problem.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Steps for Carrying Out a Waste Management Activity

pages.title: Steps for Carrying Out a Waste Management Activity
pages.body:
Assessing, planning, acting, evaluating and reporting are five general steps for carrying out a successful, sustainable waste management activity in a community, as summarised in the table below.

| **STEP** | **WHAT IT INVOLVES** |
|---|---|
| **Assess** | Identify the main sources and types of waste produced in the community |
| **Plan** | Decide which sustainable waste management approaches, such as reducing, reusing, recycling and composting, are most suitable |
| **Act** | Carry out the planned activity, such as organising a clean up exercise or setting up a composting system |
| **Evaluate** | Assess how effective the activity was, and identify what worked well and what could be improved |
| **Report** | Share findings and results with the community, school or relevant authorities |

pages.title: Evaluating Waste Management Practices
pages.body:
Effectiveness, community participation, and sustainability are three useful criteria for evaluating a waste management activity or practice carried out in a community. Effectiveness considers whether the activity actually reduced the amount of waste or improved cleanliness. Community participation considers how many people were involved and how willing they were to take part. Sustainability considers whether the practice could continue over the long term without constant external support.

For example, an activity in which a school organises a one time clean up exercise, with no follow up plan, may score well on immediate effectiveness but poorly on sustainability, while an activity that establishes a regular recycling collection point, run by community volunteers, may score well on both effectiveness and sustainability.

lessons.title: Applying Waste Management Practices in a Community (part 3)

Notice that before acting, it helps to assess which waste management approach from the hierarchy would be most suitable and achievable for your specific community, given the resources and support available.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Involving local authorities, such as a school administration or a local assembly, can strengthen the impact and sustainability of a community waste management activity, since these bodies can help provide bins, transportation for collected waste, or ongoing support after the initial activity ends. Reporting your findings clearly, using both written reports and visual aids such as photographs or charts, can also help convince others to support or continue the initiative.
